A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TrojanTO work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and the algorithms, experiments, tables, and figures can be matched despite reorganization and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original D4RL attack experiments, baseline comparisons, component ablations, and persistent-attack and trigger-perturbation results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds defense evaluations, repeated-trigger experiments, raw model returns, and a loss-formulation ablation.

M1.justification: Trajectory filtering, single-transition batch poisoning, alternating trigger/model optimization, losses, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. The post-training framing and new loss-formulation ablation clarify and evaluate the existing procedure rather than introduce a new TrojanTO component.

E1.justification: The same six D4RL datasets and task domains remain. Appendix E adds long-term return manipulation under periodic and sustained trigger activation, extending the tested scenario beyond the retained experiments on action persistence following a single trigger.

E2.justification: Baffle and IMC remain the main attack comparators. v2 adds an evaluated defense suite comprising activation-based and magnitude-based pruning, provable subspace defense, spectral analysis, activation clustering, and clean fine-tuning (Section 6.5 and Appendix B.1). These methods were not experimentally compared in v1.

E3.justification: New protocols include pruning-rate and projection-dimension sweeps, detection thresholds, clean fine-tuning, trigger-interval/length tests, and a single-objective control. Appendix C.2 also introduces BTP clipping to [0,1], whereas v1 states an unclipped ratio. Some retained appendix values contradict this rule; the PDFs do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds extensive defense analyses, an activation t-SNE visualization, repeated-trigger analysis of long-term damage, and a joint-versus-single-objective ablation in Appendix J.1. The earlier component, poisoning-budget, alternating-frequency, persistent-attack, and trigger-noise analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The main experiments retain three-seed averaging and existing uncertainty displays. New Table 15 reports averages over five seeds, while Appendix B.1 explicitly restricts defense experiments to fixed seed 1. These are reporting practices for added experiments, not evidence of increased repetitions for retained results.

E6.justification: v2 adds defense outcomes, raw returns, activation-pattern results, and loss-ablation scores. For example, Table 18 reports ASR 0.474 for single-objective versus 0.667 for joint optimization. Main average ASR/BTP/CP remains 0.719/0.914/0.701. Table 4 changes TrojanTO's GDT/Walk BTP from 1.089 to 1.000, although Appendix Table 23 retains 1.089.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 revises the RTG definition and indexing, replacing v1's target-return subtraction through the current reward with a future-reward sum and an explicit evaluation recurrence. v2 also specifies L2 distance and adds bounded BTP through clipping. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central claims of the first action-level attack against TO models, low poisoning budget, and applicability to DT/GDT/DC remain. v2 explicitly adds a novel post-training attack paradigm to its contributions and emphasizes the computational impracticality of training-time attacks on larger models.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for defense failures, including destructive subspace projection and activation variation across input types masking trigger effects. It interprets repeated triggers as enabling policy-level disruption and explains the joint loss's role. The previous defense-research limitation is replaced by a limitation concerning image observations and physically plausible triggers; residual effects after fine-tuning are also discussed.

D1.justification: v2 documents defense implementations and explains that collection of ten attack trajectories is simulated by sampling the supplied dataset. It adds a supplementary-code statement, revises experiment-count accounting from 972 to 540, and removes the 3–8-hour training-time estimate. Core hyperparameters, hardware types, and the repository URL remain.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix A.1 substantially reposition TrojanTO within post-training and model-supply-chain attacks, distinguishing it from Baffle and training-loop poisoning. New citations cover weight poisoning, handcrafted backdoors, supply-chain security, defenses, and recent RL attacks. Existing material on other RL threats is largely relocated to Appendix A.2.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, threat model, and attack explanations are substantially rewritten. Related work moves from near the conclusion to Section 2 and Appendix A; limitations and ethics are reorganized into Appendix B. A reproducibility statement and expanded explanatory sections materially change the narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 adds defense tables, raw-return and trigger-activation tables, a loss-formulation table, and t-SNE Figure 3. Existing plots and tables are retained with relocation, resizing, and revised highlighting. The conference template also changes headings, headers, typography, and page layout throughout.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves mitigation largely as future work; v2 supplies direct evidence about defense effectiveness and benign-performance costs. Table 11 shows fine-tuning reducing ASR from 1.000 to 0.040 while BTP changes from 0.964 to 0.917. Repeated-trigger tests and the loss ablation further strengthen the security assessment and methodological support. These are substantial gains, although single-seed defenses and inconsistent application of BTP clipping limit the expanded conclusions.
